The first national Mother’s Day took place on May 10, 1914. Wilson’s Proclamation 1268 directed Americans to mark the second Sunday in May with displays of the U.S. flag “as a public expression of our love and reverence for the mothers of our country.” [...] Mother’s Day became a national holiday in 1914, when President Woodrow Wilson called on Americans to honor mothers on the second Sunday in May. His proclamation came after decades of women campaigning for official recognition for the holiday. Although united in their cause, early advocates disagreed on the date.

Julia Ward Howe, a Boston-based poet, suffragist and abolitionist, called for a post-Civil War “Mother’s Day for Peace” in her 1870 Mother’s Day Proclamation. results.title: History of Mother's Day: How Mother's Day Came to Be | The Old Farmer's Almanac
results.content:
In 1887, Mary Towles Sasseen—a teacher in Henderson, Kentucky—led her class in what is the first known observance of a Mother’s Day, focusing just on honoring mothers. Later, Mary published a pamphlet about her vision for the special day to share with others. She traveled across the country to educational gatherings to promote the observance as a national holiday, primarily in public schools, with a suggested date of April 20, her mother’s birthday. Schools in several states, including [...] In 1914, President Woodrow Wilson signed a bill designating the second Sunday in May as a legal holiday to be called “Mother’s Day”—dedicated “to the best mother in the world, your mother.” For the first few years, the day was observed as a legal holiday, but in absolute simplicity and reverence—church services were held in honor of all mothers, living and dead.
